title: Diwali: the row of lamps
hookLine: Ayodhya lights a lamp on every doorstep for Rama: from darkness, lead me to light
carry: from darkness, lead me to light
last: SHAKTI: THE DIVINE MOTHER IS THE POWER IN ALL.

lines: SO HE CAN FIND HIS WAY.
cards: No moon at all. And on that night, a whole city does the opposite of sleeping. Every doorstep, every windowsill, every wall gets a small clay lamp, a little cup of oil with a cotton wick.
The story many families tell their children is simple: Rama is coming home after fourteen years, and the people of Ayodhya light the way so he can find it in the dark.
Valmiki's own telling doesn't mention the lamps; they're the festival's telling. Today, why they burn.

teach.h: BHARATA WAITS. SANDALS ON THE THRONE.
teach.b: First, the story as families tell it. Fourteen years earlier, Rama left Ayodhya for the forest so his father could keep a promise.

His brother Bharata wouldn't take the throne; he set Rama's sandals on it and ruled as their keeper, and vowed that if Rama wasn't back the day the fourteen years ran out, he'd walk into fire. So the whole city waits.
In the telling children hear, Rama comes home on amavasya, the new-moon night, and so he won't miss the road, the people put a lamp on every doorstep.
Deepa, lamp; avali, a row: Deepavali. Many teachers say the darkest night is the point. In Hindu teaching the deepest dark isn't outside.

teach.h: AVIDYA: THE DARK OF NOT KNOWING.
teach.b: It's avidya, not knowing who you really are, and the light is knowing God and the self, the atman, that shines in you.
One of the oldest prayers, from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, asks for exactly that: tamaso ma jyotir gamaya.

teach.h: FROM DARKNESS, LEAD ME TO LIGHT.
teach.b: From darkness, lead me to light. Many read every Diwali lamp as that prayer, said with a flame.
That's why, in many Hindu homes, a small lamp is lit at the shrine every evening at dusk, often with a short prayer to the light. Diwali is that evening lamp, lit by a whole city.
And it meets a dark week of your own the same way: the tradition doesn't say cheer up. It says light one lamp, and ask to see what's true.
The night is shared, too: Lakshmi is welcomed through lit doors, Jains mark Mahavira's liberation, and Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas.

how: At Diwali, Hindu families clean and decorate their homes, draw rangoli at the door, light rows of clay oil lamps, worship Lakshmi on the new-moon night, share sweets and visit relatives; in many homes a small lamp is also lit at the shrine every evening at dusk.

o: a row of lamps, lit on the new-moon night
a festival of colors at the start of spring
a night vigil kept awake for Shiva

s: Diwali's main night falls on a full moon
it falls on amavasya, the new moon: the darkest night of the month, on purpose.
for many teachers, the darkness the lamp drives out is avidya, not knowing
the light is knowing God and the self: the Upanishad's 'from darkness, lead me to light'.
for Jains it's the night Mahavira attained liberation.

games.q: it's dusk at Nani's house, and she lights the small lamp at the shrine, like every evening. a cousin asks: isn't the lamp just for Diwali? what fits today's teaching?
o: Diwali is this same evening lamp, lit by a whole city.
yes, lamps are only for festivals.
it's just there to look nice.
games.why: many homes light a lamp at dusk every day. Diwali takes that one flame, the prayer for light over the dark of not knowing, and puts it on every doorstep.

practice: Many Hindu homes light a small lamp at dusk. If it's safe, light a candle or a lamp, turn off the other lights, and look at the flame. On each slow breath out, say inwardly: tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, from darkness, lead me to light.
If you don't pray, ask the question under it instead: what am I not seeing clearly yet? Stay with the flame until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Diwali. Deepavali, a row of lamps on the darkest night: the old prayer, from darkness lead me to light, set on every doorstep.

orig.note: Sanskrit dīpāvalī: dīpa (lamp) + āvalī (row). Diwali is the everyday form.

carryVoice: Your line: from darkness, lead me to light. Diwali is the evening lamp, lit by a whole city. Day six hundred seventy-three counts.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Bharata rules with Rama's sandals and vows to enter fire if Rama does not return on time)
Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 125–128 (the homecoming, told on day 662; the lamps belong to the festival's telling)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.28 (asato mā sad gamaya, tamaso mā jyotir gamaya, mṛtyor mā amṛtaṃ gamaya)
Diwali practice: Lakshmi puja, rangoli, the evening lamp at the household shrine (Indian festival and household practice)
